mcq.q: A distributed system is best defined as:
o: One powerful computer with many CPU cores
A collection of independent computers that appears to its users as a single coherent system
A network of computers sharing one physical memory
Any computer connected to the Internet
mcq.e: Independent nodes, message passing, one coherent view (slide 16).

mcq.q: How do nodes in a distributed system coordinate?
o: Solely by passing messages over a network
Through a shared hard disk only
mcq.e: No shared memory and no global clock, so messages are the only way.

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the six core characteristics on slide 17?
mcq.e: The characteristic is NO global clock.

mcq.q: Scaling 'horizontally' means:
o: Adding more RAM to one server
mcq.e: Horizontal = scale out = more machines. Vertical = scale up = bigger machine.

mcq.q: A failure in which some nodes fail while others keep running is called:
mcq.e: Partial failures are a key challenge (slide 19).

mcq.q: In the CAP theorem, 'Availability' means:
o: Every node sees the same data at the same time
Every request gets a response, even if some nodes are down
mcq.e: The response may not contain the latest write.

mcq.q: During a network partition, a CP system will:
o: Answer every request with possibly stale data
Refuse or delay some requests to keep data consistent
mcq.e: It gives up availability to keep consistency.

mcq.q: According to the slides, banking systems usually favour:
mcq.e: A balance must be the same everywhere; social feeds favour availability.

mcq.q: Why is CA rarely a real option for distributed systems?
o: Network partitions will happen, so partition tolerance cannot be given up
CA is the default for all clouds
mcq.e: CA only fits a single site with no network split.

mcq.q: Which transparency hides that several copies of a resource exist?
mcq.e: Replication transparency.

mcq.q: In a peer-to-peer architecture:
o: Every node acts as both client and server
Clients never talk to each other
mcq.e: Peers are equal; e.g. BitTorrent.

mcq.q: A main weakness of the client-server model is:
o: The server is a bottleneck and single point of failure
mcq.e: Control and load are centralized at the server.

mcq.q: In synchronous (blocking) communication the sender:
mcq.e: Asynchronous senders continue immediately.

mcq.q: Which failure type includes malicious or arbitrary behaviour?
mcq.e: Byzantine (arbitrary) failures are the hardest to tolerate.

mcq.q: A response that is correct but arrives too late is a:
mcq.e: Timing failure: outside the specified time interval.

mcq.q: Replaying a recorded valid message later is called a:
mcq.e: Defend with timestamps/nonces and secure channels.

mcq.q: In Google's architecture, which component splits huge computations into small parallel tasks?
mcq.e: GFS stores data in replicated chunks; MapReduce processes it.

mcq.q: In MapReduce word count, the step that groups all (word,1) pairs by word is:
mcq.e: Map emits pairs, shuffle groups by key, reduce sums.

mcq.q: AWS availability zones exist so that applications can:
o: Survive the loss of an entire facility
mcq.e: AZs have independent power, cooling and networking.

mcq.q: Openness in a distributed system means:
o: The system uses published, standard interfaces so components can be added or replaced
mcq.e: E.g. HTTP, TCP/IP, REST APIs.

mcq.q: The final exam for INTE 22253 is:
mcq.e: 50% final exam, 2 hours, closed book (slide 3).

written.q: Define a distributed system and explain three of its characteristics. (6 marks)
written.a: A distributed system is a collection of independent computers that appears to its users as a single coherent system, communicating over a network to achieve a common goal. (1) Resource sharing: hardware, data and services are shared across nodes, e.g. a shared file server. (2) Concurrency: many nodes process requests simultaneously, so shared data must be protected from conflicting updates. (3) No global clock: each node has its own clock, so ordering events requires explicit coordination. (Others: scalability, fault tolerance, transparency.)

written.q: Compare horizontal and vertical scaling. Why do distributed systems prefer horizontal scaling? (4)
written.a: Vertical scaling (scale up) adds CPU/RAM to one machine; horizontal scaling (scale out) adds more machines. Horizontal scaling is preferred because there is no ceiling set by one machine's hardware, commodity servers are cheaper, and with many nodes there is no single point of failure.

written.q: State the CAP theorem. Explain with an example why a banking system and a social media feed make different choices. (6)
written.a: A distributed system can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance at once. Since partitions always happen, the real choice during a partition is C or A. A bank chooses C (CP): if replicas cannot communicate it refuses or delays requests rather than show a wrong balance, because an incorrect balance causes financial loss. A social feed chooses A (AP): it keeps answering with possibly stale posts, because a slightly old feed is acceptable but being unavailable loses users.

written.q: What is meant by "partial failure"? Why does it make distributed systems harder than centralized ones? (4)
written.a: A partial failure is when some components fail while others continue. In a centralized system failure is all-or-nothing. In a distributed system a node cannot easily tell whether another node crashed, is slow, or the network dropped the message, so it must use timeouts, retries and replication, and must avoid leaving work half-done.

Location (user does not know where a resource is), replication (does not know there are several copies), failure (does not notice a component failing and recovering), concurrency (does not notice other users sharing the resource). Also access and migration.

written.q: Compare the client-server and peer-to-peer architectures. (6)
written.a: Client-server: dedicated servers provide services and clients request them; control is centralized, simple to manage and secure, but the server is a bottleneck and single point of failure. P2P: every peer acts as both client and server; it scales naturally because each peer adds capacity and has no central SPOF, but it is harder to manage, search and secure, and must cope with peers joining and leaving.

written.q: Distinguish synchronous and asynchronous communication. Give one advantage of each. (4)
written.a: Synchronous: the sender blocks until the reply arrives — simple to program and reason about. Asynchronous: the sender continues immediately and handles the reply later — better throughput, and the sender is not stuck if the receiver is slow.

written.q: Describe four failure models. Which is hardest to tolerate and why? (5)
written.a: Crash (process stops), omission (message not sent/received), timing (correct response outside the time limit), Byzantine (arbitrary, possibly malicious behaviour). Byzantine is hardest because a faulty node may send different wrong answers to different nodes, so it cannot be detected by silence alone; the others must cross-check and vote.

written.q: Using Google, AWS or banking as an example, explain how a distributed system achieves fault tolerance and performance. (6)
written.a: Google: GFS splits files into chunks and replicates each chunk on several machines, so losing one machine loses no data (fault tolerance); MapReduce splits a job into many small tasks run in parallel on thousands of commodity servers (performance), re-running any task whose machine fails.

written.q: List three advantages and three challenges of distributed systems. (6)
written.a: Advantages: scalability, fault tolerance (no SPOF), performance via parallelism (also resource efficiency, geographic reach, cost-effective growth). Challenges: complexity, partial failures, consistency of replicated data (also synchronization without a global clock, security attack surface, network unreliability).
